pages.title: Before We Begin
pages.html:
CONVERSATIONS

OF A

DEALER

Real conversations. Real weight. The things said and unsaid in the life of someone who chose a particular kind of work and lived with everything that choice produced.

Little Bunny

PLT Press · Creative Non-Fiction

Copyright © Craig Jones / PLT Press. All rights reserved.

This is a work of creative non-fiction. The conversations documented here are based on real exchanges, reconstructed from memory, observation, and record. Some identifying details have been changed. The truth of the exchanges has not been changed.

First Edition

The work was never the point.

The people were always the point.

The conversations are what remain.

— Little Bunny

Before

Why this book exists

I was a dealer for long enough to understand that the work was not the interesting part.

The interesting part was the conversations. Who came to me and what they were actually looking for. What they said and what they meant. The way a person's whole situation — their marriage, their job, their relationship to the part of themselves they did not show anyone — arrived in the specifics of how they asked for what they wanted.

I have been thinking about those conversations for years. Not the transactions — those blur together — but the specific exchanges that carried weight. The woman who came every two weeks for three years and on the last visit told me something about her life that I have never repeated to anyone. The young man who was clearly terrified the first time and came back six more times before he stopped coming, and each time he was a little less terrified and a little more something else. The man who had been coming to me for eighteen months and one evening said, very quietly, that he thought he had a problem, and what he was really asking was whether I agreed.

I agreed. That conversation is in this book.

These are not stories about the drug trade. They are not stories about crime or consequence or the sociological weight of the work I was doing. Those stories exist and other people have written them. These are stories about the conversations that happened inside that work — the human exchanges, the moments of genuine contact, the things that got said in the specific privacy of a transaction between two people who were not supposed to know each other but did.

The PLT framework was not built when I was doing this work. It was built after, partly from observing what was happening in these conversations — what was being exchanged, what was being built, what was accruing as debt in the lives of the people I was talking to. Reading the score was something I did before I had language for it. This book gives the language to what I was already seeing.

I have changed names and details. I have not changed the truth of what was said.

— Little Bunny

pages.title: ONE
pages.html:
ONE

The First Customer

What I learned in the first week

His name was Andre. He was the first person who bought from me who was not someone I already knew, and he came through a referral that I did not fully understand the provenance of.

He was older than I expected. Somewhere in his fifties, dressed in a way that suggested he had come directly from an office — button-down shirt, dress shoes, a watch that was not extravagant but was precise. He looked at me for a long moment before he said anything, and I understood that he was making an assessment that was more careful than mine.

Andre: "You're younger than I expected."

Me: "You're older than I expected."

He smiled. The smile said: this one has some nerve, which is the first thing I need to know about someone I'm about to trust with information about my private life.

Andre: "How long have you been doing this?"

I told him the truth, which was not long. He nodded as if this was the expected answer and not necessarily a problem.

Andre: "I've been getting from the same person for four years. He moved. Someone gave me your name. I'm not looking to establish something complicated. I come, I get what I need, I go. I don't want to know about you and I don't need you to know about me."

Me: "That works for me."

Andre: "Good. One thing. I pay what things are worth. Not more, because I'm not trying to buy goodwill. Not less, because I'm not that kind of person. If I think something is wrong I'll tell you directly."

This was the clearest statement of transactional terms I received from anyone in all the years I did this work. No sentiment, no performed friendliness, no implication of anything beyond what was being described. He was telling me exactly how the relationship would run, in complete sentences, before we had done a single piece of business together.

I came to think of that conversation as the template for what a clean professional exchange looks like. He came every two weeks, reliably, for as long as I operated. He paid what things were worth. He told me directly when something was wrong. He never asked about my life and never offered information about his own, and the absence of that layer was not coldness — it was precision. He knew what the relationship was. He had decided what it would be before he arrived. He held that decision for years without ambiguity or drift.

I have tried to run every significant professional relationship in my life since then with the same clarity he brought to the first one.

— ◆ —

What I learned in the first week, from Andre: the person who tells you exactly how they want to operate at the beginning of a relationship is doing you the highest-value favor available in any exchange. They are giving you the information that makes the relationship predictable. Predictable is not the same as simple. It means the terms are known. The terms being known is everything.

pages.title: TWO
pages.html:
TWO

What She Was Looking For

The woman who came every two weeks

She came every two weeks for three years. I will call her Cora, which is not her name.

Cora was in her early forties when she first came to me, which made her significantly older than most of the people who came to my door during that period. She was composed in a way that I came to recognize as the composure of someone who had needed to be composed for a long time — not natural ease, managed steadiness. The kind of steadiness that takes significant effort and that, seen from close enough, has a quality of weight to it.

She did not explain herself on the first visit. She asked a few practical questions, paid, left. The second visit was the same. The third visit, she stayed a few minutes longer than the transaction required, and I understood that she was deciding something.

Cora: "Can I ask you something?"

Me: "Go ahead."

Cora: "Do you ever think about the people who come here? I mean — do you think about what it means. That they come here."

I told her the truth: yes, I thought about it. I thought about it more than she probably imagined.

Cora: "My husband doesn't know I do this. He would say I was self-medicating. He would be right. I am self-medicating. I'm medicating something that I don't talk about. I'm not telling you what it is. But I want you to know that I know what I'm doing."

I did not ask what she was medicating. I understood that the disclosure was not an invitation to inquire further. It was a statement of her own awareness — she was telling me that she was not operating from ignorance of her situation, and that the distinction mattered to her.

Me: "I'm not here to tell you what to do."

Cora: "I know. That's part of why I can tell you that."

— ◆ —

She came for three years. Over that time, without my asking anything and without seeming to plan what she said, she disclosed her situation in small pieces.

Her marriage was what she called functional — a word she used precisely, the way a person uses a word they have chosen carefully to carry a specific load. It functioned. It produced a shared life, shared children, shared financial stability. It did not produce what she was looking for in the two weeks between visits, which she described once, briefly, as the feeling of a door opening.

"The rest of my life is very closed," she said. "I manage things. I hold things together. This is the one thing I do that is just for the opening."

On her last visit she told me she was moving. She said it the way she said everything — composed, precise, with the particular steadiness that I had come to understand was not easy. She thanked me. Not for the product. For something she did not name specifically and that I understood to be the specific quality of the exchange we had maintained — the information that had moved between us in small pieces over three years and that had been received without judgment or advice or any implication that she should do something different with it.

"You never once told me what I should do," she said.

"It wasn't my information to do anything with," I said.

She nodded. That was the end of the conversation. It has been one of the most useful conversations I have carried in my thinking about what genuine regard looks like in practice — not the advice, not the solution, not the intervention. The quality of attention that receives what is given without converting it into a problem to be solved.

pages.title: THREE
pages.html:
THREE

The Terrified One

Six visits and a disappearance

He was nineteen and terrified on the first visit. I do not mean anxious. I mean the particular fear of someone who is doing something they have decided to do and are afraid not of getting caught but of who they will be after they have done it.

His name was Marcus — I will use his real first name because he does not read books like this and there is nothing in these pages that could find him if he did. He had the quality of someone who had been told his whole life that certain things were forbidden, not because they were harmful but because they were the kind of thing that changed you, and the change was the thing that was forbidden. He stood in my doorway as if the threshold had weight.

Marcus: "Is this... I mean, is this where—"

Me: "Yes. Come in."

He came in. He stood in the middle of the room and looked at what was available with an expression I can only describe as grieving — not for himself, but for the version of himself that would exist after this. He had not bought anything yet. He was already in mourning for something.

Me: "You don't have to be here if you don't want to be here."

Marcus: "I know. I want to be here. I just... I thought it would be different."

Me: "Different how?"

Marcus: "More... I don't know. More like something."

He bought a small amount. He left quickly. He came back six days later, which was faster than the rhythm I usually saw from first-time customers who had ambivalence about being there. The second time he was less terrified and more something I recognized as relief — the relief of someone who had found that crossing a line they had feared crossing did not produce the catastrophe they had been promised.

— ◆ —

He came six times over two months. Each visit he stayed slightly longer, asked slightly more questions, was slightly more comfortable. The comfort was not, I thought, about the product — it was about the permission structure. He had been living inside a set of prohibitions that had shaped his understanding of what kind of person he was, and each visit was a small revision of that understanding.

On the sixth visit he said something that I have thought about many times since.

Marcus: "I don't think I'm going to keep doing this. Not because of anything you did. Just — I figured out what I was looking for. I don't think it's here."

Me: "What were you looking for?"

Marcus: "Permission. To be something I wasn't supposed to be."

He was quiet for a moment.

Marcus: "I think I have to find that somewhere else. Somewhere that actually has it."

He left and did not come back. I have thought about that conversation in the context of every person I have known who was looking for permission rather than the thing they said they were looking for. The honest transaction is the one where both parties understand what is actually being exchanged. Marcus, by the sixth visit, understood what he was actually looking for. He understood that my door was not where it was available. That understanding was, I think, the most valuable thing he got from the six visits, and it cost him the price of admission six times to arrive at it.

I hope he found the place that had it.

pages.title: FOUR
pages.html:
FOUR

The Man Who Said He Had a Problem

The conversation I was least prepared for

His name is not something I will put here. I will call him what he called himself in a certain kind of mood: the Professor, because he taught at a university and because there was something in his bearing that said he had spent a long time in rooms where he was the authority.

He had been coming to me for eighteen months when it happened. A Tuesday. He came at the time he usually came, bought what he usually bought, and then instead of leaving he sat down. I had a single chair in the space I was operating from at that time. He sat in it. I leaned against the wall. He looked at the floor for a while.

Professor: "Can I ask you something?"

Me: "Go ahead."

Professor: "Do you think I have a problem?"

He asked it the way a person asks a question they already know the answer to but cannot accept until someone outside their own head confirms it. I had seen this before — the external confirmation need, the way a known truth becomes real only when it is spoken by someone who is not you.

I thought about the honest answer. The honest answer was yes — not based on any particular dramatic evidence but based on the accumulation of eighteen months of observations. The way he arrived. The specific quality of his need for the visits to be on schedule. The thing that happened to his posture in the first ten minutes after he had what he came for versus what it was when he arrived. None of it was catastrophic. All of it was consistent. Yes, I thought he had a problem.

Me: "Yes."

He nodded. The nod was not surprise. It was recognition — the feeling of a truth landing in a place it had been circling for a long time.

Professor: "What kind of problem?"

Me: "The kind where you need this more than it needs to be needed. Where the visit is the thing you're organizing your week around and not the other things."

Professor: "Yes."

Long silence.

Professor: "I've known for about four months. I haven't been able to say it."

Me: "You just said it."

Professor: "I said it to you."

Me: "That's a start."

— ◆ —

He left that evening and came back two more times before he stopped coming. On the second-to-last visit he told me he had made an appointment with someone. On the last visit he said he was going to stop. He said it plainly, as a statement rather than a resolution — he was not asking me to hold him accountable or to celebrate the decision. He was informing me that the visits would end, which was both a courtesy and, I think, a form of practice. If he could say it to me, he could say it to someone whose response to the statement would have more weight.

That conversation stays with me for a specific reason. He asked me a question that I was uniquely positioned to answer honestly — I had been observing him for eighteen months from a position of total non-judgment, which gave me a particular kind of clarity about what I was seeing. And the honest answer was the thing he needed in order to move. He had been unable to say the thing to himself. He could receive it from someone outside.

This is, in the PLT framework, the Evidence Mirror in its most human form. He handed me the question. I reflected the evidence back. The reflection produced the movement that his own internal evidence had not been able to produce. The score of that exchange was the highest Love score I produced in all the years I did this work, and it came in the conversation where I agreed with someone that they had a problem I was part of creating.

That contradiction has sat in me for a long time. It is still sitting.

pages.title: FIVE
pages.html:
FIVE

The One Who Knew Everyone

The social customer and what she taught me about trust

I will call her Renee. She was the most socially fluent person who came through my door, which in a world where social fluency is a survival skill meant she was very socially fluent. She knew everyone. Not in the casual sense — she knew them specifically: their situations, their needs, the precise nature of what they were managing and what they were hiding. She was not a gossip. She was an observer who happened to share what she observed with someone she had decided to trust, which happened to be me.

The first time she came she gave me a ten-minute overview of the person who had referred her — what they were like, where they were reliable and where they were not, what they wanted from people and what they gave back. It was precise, specific, and generous — she was not being unkind about the person who had sent her, she was giving me information she thought would be useful.

Me: "You told me a lot about somebody who sent you here."

Renee: "I wanted you to know what you're connected to. Who vouches for you matters. I wanted you to know exactly what kind of vouch that is."

This was, I came to understand, how Renee operated in all of her relationships. She gave information that was useful at the beginning because she had decided the relationship was worth having, and the information was the investment. If you were going to be connected to her network of observation and trust, you needed to know the quality of what you were connected to.

Renee: "One thing I'll tell you now. I don't repeat what I hear in rooms like this. Not ever. I expect the same."

Me: "That's already how I work."

Renee: "Good. I know several people who work differently. You'll meet some of them eventually and you'll be tempted to share what you know because knowing something other people don't know feels like currency. It's not currency. It's debt."

— ◆ —

She was right. I watched people in this work trade in information about their customers and I watched them lose everything when the trading came back to its source, which it always did. The information that feels like currency is always debt — it is borrowed credibility that must be repaid with interest when the person it was borrowed from discovers the borrowing.

Renee came for two years. The conversations we had during her visits were, over time, the most sophisticated discussions of human behavior and motivation that I had with anyone during that period of my life. She thought carefully about why people did what they did, and she communicated her thinking precisely, and she was right often enough that I developed a habit of paying close attention whenever she said anything.

On one of her visits she said something that became one of the organizing principles of the PLT framework, though I did not have the framework yet when she said it.

Renee: "The reason people don't trust each other is not that they've been betrayed. It's that they've been right too many times about knowing they would be."

She left it there. I have been thinking about it since.

pages.title: SIX
pages.html:
SIX

The Couple

What a relationship looks like from the outside

They came together twice, separately several times each, and the pattern of those visits told me more about their relationship than either of them disclosed in any single conversation.

I will call them Terrence and Diana. They came together the first time and the register between them was immediately legible: she had proposed the visit, he had agreed to it, and his agreement was the kind that carries a residue of reluctance that has been managed rather than resolved. He was present. He was not entirely there.

The second time they came together, the register had shifted. He was the one who proposed the timing. She was the one who followed. I noticed this without commenting on it. A lot of what I observed in this work I noticed without commenting on.

Over the months that followed, they came separately more often than together. I watched the separate visits accumulate and thought about what the visits represented in the architecture of a relationship — what it meant that each of them was making a specific kind of space for themselves inside a shared life.

Diana: "Can I ask you something strange?"

Me: "Go ahead."

Diana: "Does Terrence seem okay when he comes?"

I considered the question carefully. She was not asking whether Terrence was using more than she knew about — she was asking about his emotional register. Whether he seemed like someone who was holding something.

Me: "I don't talk about people who come through here."

Diana: "I know. I'm asking... not specifically. Just in general. When you see someone regularly, do you notice when something is different with them?"

Me: "Yes."

Diana: "Is something different with him?"

I looked at her for a moment. The question was honest and the person asking it was not trying to catch anyone in anything — she was a woman who was worried about someone she loved and who was asking in the only room where she thought she might get an answer that was not managed.

Me: "I think you should ask him directly. Not because I won't answer but because my answer isn't the one that will actually help you. You already know something is different. You came here to confirm it. Confirmation from me isn't what you need. The conversation with him is what you need."

She was quiet for a while.

Diana: "I know."

Me: "I know you know."

— ◆ —

She came twice more and then she and Terrence both stopped coming. I do not know what happened between them. I know that the conversation she needed to have was not the one she had with me but the one she was trying to prepare herself for by having it with me.

This is something I observed many times in this work: people practicing a difficult conversation with the safest available audience before they are ready to have it with the person it is actually about. The practice conversation is not the same as the real one — it does not have the same stakes or the same presence — but it sometimes produces the clarity or the resolve that the real conversation requires.

I was, in a specific way, a practice room. Not intentionally. Not by design. But the particular privacy of the exchange — the complete absence of social consequence, the certainty that nothing said would travel — made it a space where people could say things they were building toward saying somewhere else.

I came to understand that this was part of what I was providing. Not just the product. The room.

pages.title: SEVEN
pages.html:
SEVEN

The Young Ones

What I would not do and why

There were two of them. They were young — the kind of young where their youth was the most visible thing about them, preceding them into the room before they said anything.

They had been sent by someone I knew. The referral was not a recommendation — it was a handoff, which is different. A recommendation says: this person is worth your time. A handoff says: I don't want to deal with this anymore, you handle it.

They stood at my door with the particular energy of people who expected to be turned away and had already decided to be offended by it. The taller one spoke first.

Tall one: "We heard you could help us out."

I looked at them for a long moment. The shorter one had the specific quality of someone who was there because the taller one had insisted — not reluctant exactly, but not his own idea.

Me: "How old are you?"

Tall one: "Old enough."

Me: "That's not a number."

Tall one: "Eighteen."

I did not believe him. I also did not pursue the question, because the answer was not the relevant issue.

Me: "I can't help you."

Tall one: "Why not? We've got money."

Me: "That's not the issue."

Tall one: "Then what's the issue?"

Me: "You're too young. And you have the look of someone who doesn't know yet what this will cost them. I don't deal with people who don't know what something will cost them. It's bad business."

The taller one looked at me with the particular expression of someone trying to decide whether to be angry or impressed.

Tall one: "Bad business."

Me: "Bad business for me and bad for you. Come back in a few years if you still want to. You'll know more about what you're deciding."

— ◆ —

They left. I do not know if they found someone else, which they almost certainly did — the barrier to access for a determined young person is not high.

But the decision I made in that doorway was one I held through all the years I did this work, and it was grounded in something that was not entirely moral, though it was also moral. It was also practical. The person who does not understand the cost of what they are buying is not a customer — they are a liability. They are the person who, when the cost arrives, does not recognize it as the thing they agreed to. They are the person who looks for an external cause for an internal consequence.

The cost of what I sold was real and I knew it was real. The people who were equipped to manage that cost were the ones who also knew it was real and had decided they could manage it. The ones who did not know — the young, the uninformed, the people in a crisis moment who were looking for immediate relief from something that required a different kind of relief — those were not people I could help without doing something I did not want to do with my hands.

The line I held was not clean. No line in that work was clean. But it was a line, and holding it was the thing that allowed me to look at what I was doing with some clarity rather than managing my view of it.

pages.title: EIGHT
pages.html:
EIGHT

The Last Customer

How it ended

The last person who came to me as a customer was a woman I had known for almost the entire time I had been doing this work. I will not give her a name because the name I would give her would be the real one, and the real one is not mine to put here.

She had been the first person outside my immediate circle who had come to my door. She had been there close to the beginning and she was there close to the end, though she did not know it was close to the end and I had not told her yet.

On this particular visit she arrived with something different in her face — not the usual ease of someone returning to a familiar place, but the specific quality of someone who has made a decision that is sitting heavily on them.

Her: "I've been thinking about you."

Me: "About me."

Her: "About what you're doing. About how long you've been doing it. About when it ends."

I let the observation sit. She was not asking a question. She was saying something she had been building toward saying and she needed the space to say it without me filling the space with a response before she was done.

Her: "I think about what comes next for you. You're too smart for this to be the whole thing. And I know — I know you've been building something else. I can see it in you. The way you're not all the way here anymore."

Me: "Is it that visible?"

Her: "To me it is. I've been paying attention for a long time."

She was right. I had been building something else — a different kind of operation, a legitimate structure, the thing I had been moving toward for two years while still running the current work. She had seen it before I had said it to anyone.

Her: "I just want to say — whatever it is, it's going to be good. Because you're someone who pays attention. And people who pay attention build things that are worth paying attention to."

I did not say anything immediately. The compliment was specific — not 'you're smart' or 'you'll be fine' but a precise observation about a particular quality and its likely consequence.

Me: "That means something coming from you."

Her: "It's supposed to."

— ◆ —

She was the last customer I had from the world I had been building for years. Not because she stopped coming after that — she came three more times before I wound things down. But the conversation on that visit was the one that I think of as the ending, because it was the one where someone who had been paying close attention to me said the thing that named what was actually happening, which was that I was already leaving.

The conversations in this book are the reason I understand what I understand about how human exchange works. Not the transactions — those were never the interesting part. The people. The specific things they said. What they were actually looking for and how they used the particular privacy of those visits to move closer to it.

What I was looking for, in the years I did this work, was the same thing most people are looking for in whatever work they choose: to understand something. To pay close enough attention to the world in front of me that the understanding became real — not theoretical, not borrowed, mine.

These conversations are what I understand.

pages.title: NINE
pages.html:
NINE

The One I Couldn't Help

The conversation that stayed

I have held this conversation back because I have not known what to do with it. It is the one that does not resolve. It is the one where the honest accounting is uncomfortable and I cannot make it comfortable by reframing it.

He came to me during a difficult period in his life — a divorce, a job situation, something with his children that he mentioned only once and did not elaborate on. He came three times in two weeks, which was a frequency that told me something about the difficulty of the period.

On the third visit he looked like someone who had not slept properly in a while. He sat down without asking whether it was all right to sit, which was unusual — most people maintained a particular transactional posture that did not include sitting down without invitation.

Him: "I don't know what I'm doing."

He did not mean coming to see me. He meant generally. He meant the whole situation — the divorce, the job, the children, the visits to my door that were becoming more frequent.

Me: "What do you need?"

Him: "I don't know. I'm not sure this is it."

He gestured at the room — at the transaction he had come for — and what he was saying was that he had arrived at the recognition Marcus had arrived at, which was that the thing he had come looking for was not available here. But unlike Marcus, who had been young and was looking for permission, this man was looking for something I did not have a name for and neither did he.

Me: "What would it be? If it were here?"

He thought about it for a long time.

Him: "Something that made me feel like myself again. I haven't felt like myself in about eight months. Everything is — the shape of my life is completely wrong right now and I can't find my way back to the right shape."

Me: "I can't give you that."

Him: "I know."

Me: "Is there someone who can?"

He thought about it.

Him: "There's a person I should probably talk to. Someone who knows me from before everything went wrong. I've been avoiding them."

Me: "Why?"

Him: "Because talking to them means admitting how far off track I am. And I'm not sure I can do that yet."

Me: "You just told me."

He looked at me. The same recognition as with the Professor — the truth having become real by being spoken outside his own head.

Him: "I guess I did."

— ◆ —

He came back twice after that and then stopped. I do not know whether he had the conversation with the person who knew him from before. I do not know whether he found his way back to the right shape.

The conversation that stayed is not the part I have described. The part that stayed is the ending of it — what happened after he said "I guess I did."

He bought what he came for. And I sold it to him. After having just established together that what he needed was something else — after having arrived at the precise diagnosis of what was wrong and where it needed to be addressed — we concluded the transaction we had come together to conclude.

I have never made peace with that. I have thought about what I should have done differently and I cannot construct the version of that moment where I handled it well. The thing I had to sell was the thing he had come for. The thing he needed was something I could not provide. The gap between those two facts produced the transaction, and the transaction was the honest and honest-feeling and still wrong thing that happened in that room.

I write it here because the honest accounting of what this work was requires holding it. Not the moments where I declined the young ones at my door. Not the moments where I reflected the evidence that someone had a problem. This moment — the one where both of us knew what was needed and neither of us had the capacity to make it happen — this is the one that tells the truth about what the work was and what it was not.

It was not neutral. That is what I want to say. Even when it was careful. Even when it was clean. It was not neutral, and the pretense that it could be neutral was the thing I had to give up in order to leave it.

pages.title: TEN
pages.html:
TEN

What I Kept

After

I have been out of that work for long enough that it is the past tense in every way that matters. The work I do now is different in every respect except the one that was always the actual work: the conversations.

I kept the attention. The particular quality of presence that the work required — reading the room, reading the person, understanding what was actually happening in an exchange rather than what appeared to be happening — that is the thing the work gave me that has applied everywhere since.

I kept the knowledge that people are looking for something in every transaction they enter, and that the thing they are looking for is almost never the thing they said they came for. This is not a cynical observation. It is a compassionate one. The woman who came for the opening in a life that was very closed. The man who came to feel like himself again. Marcus who came for permission. The Professor who came for an external confirmation of the thing he already knew. All of them were looking for something real. The fact that what they were looking for was not fully available at my door does not mean they were wrong to look for it.

People look for things in imperfect places because the perfect place for the thing they are looking for is often unavailable — too frightening, too exposing, too dependent on relationships that have already been damaged by the thing they are managing. The imperfect place is reachable. The reachable is what people reach for.

I also kept the understanding that the honest conversation — the one where what is actually happening is named, where what is actually needed is said, where the person across from you is treated as someone whose real situation matters rather than someone whose managed presentation is accepted at face value — is the rarest and most valuable thing available in most rooms. And that the rarity is what makes it so useful when it happens.

The PLT framework is built from everything in this book. From Andre's precise statement of transactional terms. From Cora's careful disclosure of what the visits were for. From the Professor asking whether he had a problem. From Renee's observation that information that feels like currency is always debt. From the man who needed to feel like himself again and from what I did and did not give him.

Profit. Love. Tax. I was counting all three before I had the words for them. The words came later, from making explicit what the work had made visible.

The conversations are what remain. They remain in this book and they remain in me, and I carry them the way you carry the things that were true about a period of your life that you have left but that has not left you.

— Little Bunny

About the Author

Craig Jones writes under the name Little Bunny. He is the founder of the PLT Framework and the architect of the PLT Doctrine Series. Conversations of a Dealer is creative non-fiction — based on real conversations, real people, and a real period of his life. It is the book in the series that is most personal and least comfortable, which is the reason it exists.
